enunciado.texto:
TEXTO-BASE:

Local Voices, Global English

At a public secondary school in a multilingual river community, English classes were redesigned around local stories, environmental knowledge and digital exchanges with students in other regions. The teachers did not present English as a replacement for local languages. Instead, they treated it as an additional resource for communication, research and collaboration. Students compared different ways of naming plants, places and community practices, discussed how meanings change across languages, and prepared short bilingual videos for an online exhibition.

The project also exposed learners to several accents and varieties of English. Rather than asking them to imitate a single model, teachers emphasized intelligibility, respectful interaction and the ability to negotiate meaning. The approach required careful planning: online materials were checked for stereotypes, sources were discussed, and students were invited to question whose perspectives were represented. In this way, language learning became connected to identity, critical literacy and participation in a wider world.

Beyond the Worksheet

Digital tools can enrich language lessons when they are chosen for a clear learning purpose. A shared document, for example, may help students write together and notice how their choices affect a reader.
